content: I want to build an app to save and manage bookmarks.

I'll be facilitating this project through a structured cycle. We're at the very start — Phase 1, understanding what you actually want before anything gets built. Let me begin by understanding the goal, not the features.

A few questions to settle the direction:

**1. Why this, why now?**
You already have browser bookmarks, a notes app, maybe other places to stash links. What's not working about how you save links today? When this app exists and works well, what should be *different* about your daily life compared to now?

**2. What's the real job?**
"Save and manage bookmarks" can mean quite different things depending on the goal. For example — is the pain that you *lose* links you meant to keep? That you *can't find* things you saved? That your saved stuff is a messy pile you never revisit? Or something else? Which of these is closest to your actual frustration?

**3. Who is this for?**
Just you, personally? Or you and other people (a team, family, the public)?

Please answer in plain terms — don't worry about how it would be built. I just want to understand what you're really after before we look at any actual screens together.

It’s just for me. Right now I save links in browser bookmarks, notes, and open tabs, then either forget about them or can’t find them again.

I want one dependable personal place where I can quickly save a link, organize it, and later find it by searching or browsing categories. I’d also like to mark things I intend to read and keep useful links without my main view becoming cluttered. Ideally, saved pages would remain accessible even if the original changes or disappears. The real difference should be that saving something makes it genuinely retrievable and useful later, rather than sending it into another messy pile.

content:
That's a clear and helpful picture. Let me play back what I understood and check a couple of things about what's truly core versus nice-to-have.

**What I heard the goal is:**
> One dependable personal place where saving a link is quick, and what you save is *genuinely retrievable later* — through search and by browsing categories — instead of disappearing into another messy pile.

That "genuinely retrievable and useful later" is the heart of it. Before we look at any screens, two scope questions:

**1. The "stays accessible even if the original changes or disappears" part.**
This one is a big deal — it's the difference between keeping a *pointer* to a page (which can rot or vanish) and keeping an actual *copy* of what the page said. It's genuinely useful, but it's also a much heavier promise than the rest. Is that preservation:
- **essential** — a link that later goes dead is a real failure for you, or
- **a bonus** — nice if it happens, but the core value is still there without it?

I ask because it may shape a lot, and I'd rather know now whether it's part of the must-have center or something we note for later.

**2. "Mark things I intend to read" vs. "keep useful links without cluttering my main view."**
These sound like they might be two different needs:
- a *"read this soon"* pile you actively work through, and
- a *"done with it / keep for reference"* stash that's out of the way but findable.

Is that two separate things in your mind, or really one "keep it but not in my face" idea? And when you picture your **main view** — the thing you see when you open the app — what do you *want* to be looking at? Your unread things? Everything? Recent saves?

Preserving a copy is important to me, but I’d treat it as a later addition rather than hold up the useful first version.

The other two needs are separate. “Read later” is an active queue: I should be able to see only those items and mark them read when I’m done. Archiving is for links I want to keep but remove from the normal view, with a separate place where I can find and restore them.

For the main view, I’d prefer my recent, non-archived saves—not only unread items.

Instead of making a **duplicate**, it should tell you *"You've already saved this"* with a **"Show it"** link that jumps to and briefly highlights the existing one. Also try re-saving a link that's in your **Archived** tab — it should tell you it's in the archive.

Two decisions I'd like your read on:
- **Duplicates are prevented, not silently added** — the app points you to the one you already have (even if it's archived) rather than creating a second copy. Is that what you'd want, or would you rather it just let you save it again?
- **A bad address is blocked with a hint** rather than saved as-is. Right degree of strictness, or too fussy?

How do these feel?

Both feel right. I don’t want duplicate copies of the same link; pointing me to the existing bookmark, including an archived one, is much more useful. From there I can edit or restore it if needed.

Blocking clearly invalid text is also the right level of strictness, especially since ordinary addresses without `https://` are still accepted.

We've now worked through all the main flows *and* the tricky edge situations, and your recent reactions have been consistent approvals. I think we've fully explored the scope for this first version. Here's everything that's settled — this is what I'd build:

**Saving & titles**
- Paste a link, optionally add tags, save. It appears instantly, and the page's real title fills in on its own. If a title can't be read, the address stands in until you rename it.

**Organizing**
- Links carry multiple tags (not single folders). As you type a tag, your existing tags are suggested (most-used first) so you don't create near-duplicates.
- Edit a bookmark's title and tags together via the pencil, reviewing before you save.

**Finding**
- Browse by tag from the top row or from a link's own tags.
- Search across titles, addresses, and tags at once, with matches highlighted; search narrows within the tag you're browsing, and a friendly message shows when nothing matches.

**Read-later queue**
- Opt links into a "To read" queue, see only those, and "Mark read" to clear them from the queue (the bookmark stays).

**Archiving & deleting**
- Archive to tuck a link out of your normal view (and out of search/queue), with a separate Archived tab to find and restore it — one click, reversible.
- Delete permanently from inside the edit form, with a confirmation that names the link and points you to Archive as the safe alternative.

**Dependability & clean input**
- Everything persists across sessions — links, tags, read status, archive status.
- Invalid addresses are blocked with a hint; duplicates aren't re-added — you're pointed to the existing one (even if archived).
- It's your personal collection on your own device — no accounts or login in this version.

**Noted for later (not in this version):** saving a full copy of each page, per-link notes/descriptions, and an undo/trash for deletion.

That's **10 settled behaviors**. **May I now start building this as the real application?** Once you approve, I'll switch from exploring to actually implementing it.
